title: Health Records and Informatics
summary: Learn how health information is recorded and used: record standards, ICD coding, health information systems and data quality, hospital indicators, electronic records and digital health, privacy and security, and records management.
audience: Health records officers, clinic staff, data officers, health students and administrators

body.p: A health record documents a person's health history, examinations, diagnoses, treatments and outcomes. It supports continuity of care between professionals and visits, legal protection for patients and staff, billing and insurance, planning, and research.

list: Patient-held records, such as road-to-health cards for children and antenatal cards.
Facility records: outpatient registers, inpatient files, laboratory and pharmacy records.
Electronic health records (EHRs) stored in computer systems.
Aggregate reports: monthly summaries sent to district and national health information systems.
Accurate, complete and written at the time of care or soon after.
Legible, dated, timed and signed, with the writer's name and role.
Using approved terms and abbreviations only.
Never altered dishonestly: corrections follow set procedures and remain visible.
Stored securely and retained for the period required by law.

body.tip: A good record lets a colleague who has never met the patient understand what happened and what to do next.

body.p: Classifications turn written diagnoses into standard codes so data can be counted and compared across facilities and countries.

list: ICD (International Classification of Diseases), maintained by WHO, codes diseases and causes of death. Many countries still use ICD-10; ICD-11 came into effect in 2022 and countries are moving to it. For example, ICD-10 codes beginning with A15 relate to respiratory tuberculosis.
Procedure classifications code operations and interventions.
Other standards cover medicines, laboratory tests and clinical terms (such as SNOMED CT).
Code from the clinical documentation, not from assumptions.
Code the main condition treated, plus important other conditions.
Ask clinicians to clarify vague or conflicting notes.
Follow national coding rules and audit a sample regularly.

body.p: Accurate coding matters: it determines disease statistics used to plan services, and in many systems it also determines how hospitals are paid.

body.tip: Poor handwriting and vague diagnoses ("fever", "pain") become poor data; encourage specific, legible documentation.

body.p: Health information systems collect, analyse and use data to manage services. Many African countries use DHIS2, an open-source platform, to collect monthly facility reports and display them in dashboards for districts and ministries.

list: Completeness: if 46 of 50 expected facility reports arrive, completeness is 46 / 50 = 92%.
Timeliness: if 40 arrived by the deadline, timeliness is 80%.
Accuracy: numbers in reports should match the source registers; data verification exercises compare them.
Consistency: values should make sense over time and across related indicators.
Bed occupancy rate = patient-days / (beds x days). 2700 patient-days in a 100-bed hospital over 30 days is 2700 / 3000 = 90%.
Average length of stay = patient-days / discharges. 2700 / 450 = 6 days.
Bed turnover = discharges / beds = 450 / 100 = 4.5 patients per bed in the month.
Hospital death rate = deaths / discharges (including deaths). 18 / 450 = 4%.

body.tip: Use the data you collect: share simple charts with facility staff each month so they see the value of good recording.

lessons.title: Electronic health records and digital health

body.p: Electronic health records make information available to authorised staff instantly, reduce lost files and illegible notes, support alerts (such as allergy warnings) and make reporting easier. But they need reliable power, connectivity, training, maintenance and good design.

Systems must exchange data: a laboratory system sending results to a clinic's EHR, or a pharmacy system checking prescriptions. Standards such as HL7 FHIR define common formats, and unique patient identifiers link records across facilities.

list: Mobile tools for community health workers to register households and follow up patients.
SMS reminders for appointments, medication and vaccinations.
Telemedicine connecting remote clinics with specialists.
Logistics systems tracking medicine stock to prevent stock-outs.
Disease surveillance systems that detect outbreaks early.

body.tip: Introduce digital systems with the people who will use them; tools designed without users are often abandoned.

body.p: Health information is among the most sensitive personal data. Patients share it trusting that it will be protected; breaches can cause discrimination, stigma and harm, and they damage trust in health services.

list: Share information only with those involved in the patient's care, or as the law requires.
Obtain consent for other uses, such as some research, unless the law allows otherwise.
Follow data-protection laws such as POPIA in South Africa, the Nigeria Data Protection Act and Kenya's Data Protection Act, which treat health data as special or sensitive.
Give patients access to their records according to the law.
Keep paper records locked and never leave files where others can read them.
Use individual log-ins; never share passwords; lock screens when leaving.
Access only the records you need for your work; systems log who viewed what.
Encrypt devices and back up data.
Report suspected breaches immediately.

body.tip: Never discuss patients in public places such as corridors, lifts or social media, even without names.

body.p: Health records departments manage the life cycle of records: creation, indexing, storage, retrieval, retention and disposal.

list: Use a master patient index so each patient has one record and duplicates are avoided.
File systematically (for example terminal-digit filing) so records can be found quickly.
Track records that leave the department.
Retain records for the periods set by law and policy, which are often longer for children's and maternity records.
Destroy records securely when retention ends, and keep a disposal register.

body.p: Health information professionals work as records officers, clinical coders, data managers, monitoring and evaluation officers and health informaticians. Skills in data analysis, spreadsheets, databases and data protection are increasingly valued alongside medical terminology.

body.tip: Learn medical terminology and basic data analysis together; they are the foundation of most health information roles.
